tldr.text: This lesson is about assurance, the work of checking whether a control keeps its promise. It comes in levels, from owners checking their own controls up to internal and external audit, and each level is more independent than the last.

Every test answers one of two questions. A test of design asks whether the control, as designed, would meet its objective. A test of operating effectiveness asks whether it actually ran across a whole period. Design comes first.

Testers ask, watch, inspect records and re-perform the control, and asking alone never proves a control ran. Most controls run too often to check every time, so the tester picks a sample from a complete population, spread across the whole period.

Strong evidence covers every instance and the whole period, shows when and by whom, and comes straight from the system of record. Collect it as each control runs, rather than chasing screenshots before fieldwork, and gaps will surface in the month they open.

A SOC 2 Type I report looks at design on a single date, while Type II also tests operation over a period and lists any exceptions. ISO 27001 certification runs on a three-year cycle, with surveillance audits at least every year.
tldr.say: A sock two type one report looks at design on a single date, while type two also tests operation over a period and lists any exceptions. I S O twenty-seven thousand one certification runs on a three-year cycle, with surveillance audits at least every year.

tldr.text: Rate each finding by severity, find the root cause, and fix both the instance and the cause. Track it in a plan of action and milestones, and close it only when someone other than the owner retests the fix.

Next, practice choosing the stronger evidence and putting the evidence chain in order. Then take the knowledge check, and look for the difference between proving a control was designed well and proving it ran.

activities.title: Pick the stronger evidence
activities.prompt: For each of Big Venture's controls, pick the evidence that would stand up in a Type II audit.

pairs.a: An email from the reviewer saying this quarter's access reviews are done
pairs.b: An identity-system export of every account, each reviewer decision, the sign-off date and removal tickets
pairs.why: The export covers every account and shows each decision, who made it and when, while the email only claims the work was done.

pairs.a: The HR termination report matched to deactivation logs, with the time between them for each leaver
pairs.b: A hand-edited spreadsheet of the year's leavers, each one marked "done"
pairs.why: Matching HR records to deactivation logs is complete and comes from the systems of record; a hand-edited list is neither.

pairs.a: A signed policy stating that backups run every night
pairs.b: Job logs for the period and a dated restore test, with its result and who ran it
pairs.why: A policy shows intent, not operation; the logs and a dated restore test show the control ran and who ran it.

pairs.a: Audit trail entries in a log that ordinary users cannot alter
pairs.b: A copy of the log exported to a shared folder that anyone can edit
pairs.why: An auditor needs to know a record could not have been quietly edited afterwards, and a tamper-evident log gives that.

activities.title: Type I, Type II or bridge letter
activities.prompt: Big Venture's customers read several documents about its controls. Sort each statement into the one it describes.

items.text: Says whether controls were suitably designed as of a specific date
items.why: Type I looks at design at a single point in time.

items.text: Lists each test performed and its result, including any exceptions
items.why: Type II tests operation over a period and records each place a control did not operate as described.

items.text: Written by the organization's management, not by the auditor
items.why: A bridge letter comes from management, so it carries only management's word.

items.text: States whether there have been material changes since the report period ended
items.why: It fills the gap between the end of a report's period and today, which the report itself cannot cover.

items.text: Often a first report, but silent on how controls performed over time
items.why: Type I is a common starting point, but it does not test whether controls operated.

items.text: Covers whether controls operated effectively throughout a review period
items.why: Operating effectiveness over a period is what Type II adds to the design opinion.

items.text: Tested with sampling across a period of several months to a year
items.why: Sampling across a period is how operation is tested, and only Type II tests operation.

activities.title: Follow the evidence chain
activities.prompt: Put the steps of Big Venture's offboarding finding in order, from the control itself to closing the finding.
steps: The offboarding control has an owner and a clear objective
A tester checks its design, then samples leavers from across the year
Termination dates matched to deactivation logs become the evidence
Three leavers left active for a week are logged as a high-severity finding
A corrective action feeds HR terminations straight into the identity system
The second line tests every leaver since the fix and closes the finding
activities.why: Each step needs the one before it: a test produces evidence, evidence reveals the finding, and the finding gets a corrective action. It closes only when a retest of the fixed control passes; if the retest fails, the loop runs again.
